Show 112 with bundles of ten straws and loose straws, then build it again with on-screen base-ten blocks
Drag 98, 120, 104 and 111 onto an on-screen number line in order from smallest to largest

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Number Words to 100
topic.description: Read and write numbers to at least 100 in words
evidence: Read 'fifty-seven' and write the numeral 57
Write 'eighty-three' when shown the numeral 83
Read and write all decade words (twenty, thirty … ninety) correctly
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write 'seventy-four' or 'one hundred and three' as number words — and read them correctly when they appear in a book or on a sign?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (LANGUAGE): read and write numbers to at least 100 in WORDS — extending the number-word vocabulary to decade words and two-word compounds (fifty-seven), mapping word↔numeral↔quantity.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'read and write numbers to at least 100 in numerals and in words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.3 'read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form' (the 0–100 word range sits within this).
• Operational details — building on words to twenty, the child learns the DECADE words (twenty, thirty ... ninety) and the hyphenated compound structure 'tens-word + ones-word' (fifty-seven = 57). The English pattern above twenty is regular and tens-first (unlike the teens), so the main work is (i) the decade spellings, (ii) the fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty confusions, and (iii) hyphenation and word↔numeral order.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): read 'fifty-seven' and write 57. Tier B (6–7): write 'eighty-three' when shown 83. Tier C (7): read and write all decade words and compound words to 100 correctly, spelling and hyphenating them.
bestPractices: Teach the DECADE words as a set (twenty…ninety) and their link to the tens digit, then the regular compound rule 'decade-word + ones-word' (sixty-four) — above twenty the words are tens-first and regular, a helpful contrast with the teens.
Drill the sound-alike traps directly: thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty, etc. — pair each with its numeral and a quantity so meaning disambiguates the near-identical words.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity (read 'seventy-two' → write 72 → show ~72 on a line) so the words carry meaning, not just spelling.
Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds (forty-five), the tricky spellings (forty not fourty, ninety), coordinating with spelling/handwriting teaching.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.
keyRepresentations: Decade-word chart (20–90) linked to the tens digit and to bundles of tens.
Word-building frame: [decade word] + [ones word] → compound (sixty + four → sixty-four) beside 64.
Triple-match cards: numeral ↔ word ↔ quantity/number-line position.
Sound-alike contrast pairs (thirteen|thirty, fifteen|fifty) each with a set/numeral.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing '-teen' and '-ty' words by sound and spelling (fifteen vs fifty, thirteen vs thirty).
Misspelling irregular decades (forty as 'fourty', ninety as 'ninty').
Omitting the hyphen or writing compounds as one/many words incorrectly.
Transposing compound numbers back to numerals (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — carrying over the teen ones-first habit.
Writing decade words with extra zeros from the spoken parts (fifty-seven → 507).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: reading and writing numbers to at least 100 in words, extending from number words to twenty into the decade words (twenty, thirty … ninety) and two-word hyphenated compounds (fifty-seven). The central work is mapping word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity, learning commonly misspelled decade words (forty drops the u of four; ninety keeps the e of nine), fixing the hyphen, and untangling the sound-alike '-teen'/'-ty' pairs (fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty). Above twenty the English words follow a regular tens-first pattern (decade word, then ones word), a useful contrast with the teens, although some decade stems (twenty, thirty, fifty, forty) are spelled irregularly.

activities.title: Build compound number words from decade + ones parts
feedback: If a learner writes 'eighty-three' as 803, show that eighty-three means 8 tens and 3 ones: build it and place the 3 into the ones column of a tens/ones frame so it does not trail after 80.
If the compound is run together or missing the hyphen, point to the two parts (decade word + ones word) and show the hyphen joins exactly those two words.
If the order is reversed (writing 'forty-two' as 24), re-read the word tens-first: 'forty' is the tens, '-two' is the ones, so the tens digit comes first (42).
If a decade word is misspelled ('fourty', 'ninty'), flag the correct spelling (forty, ninety) and keep it visible as a reference.
activities.rationale: Composing the word from decade and ones parts and mapping it to both numeral and quantity makes the regular tens-first structure explicit and keeps the words meaningful rather than rote spellings. An optional on-screen builder where tiles snap to the numeral and a number-line position can make this mapping concrete, but the same can be done with word-part cards and a drawn line.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Choose a decade-word part (e.g. 'sixty') and a ones-word part (e.g. 'four') and join them into the compound word 'sixty-four', writing it with the hyphen.

Write the numeral64 beside sixty-four and locate it on a0–100 line. Optionally join on-screen tens and ones word tiles so the compound immediately links to its numeral and line position, with a reverse round asking the learner to assemble or spell the word for83.
Work the reverse direction: shown the numeral 83, say and then correctly spell the word 'eighty-three'.
Write seventy-eight, seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, then ninety-nine and one hundred. Notice when a decade changes, when a hyphenated compound is used, and how100 is written.
activities.intendedInsight: For numbers from21 to99 with a nonzero ones digit, the English word is a tens-first compound, such as sixty-four. Exact tens use the decade word alone, and100 is one hundred; connect each form to its numeral and quantity.

activities.title: Sound-alike contrast: '-teen' versus '-ty'
feedback: If a learner uses fifteen and fifty interchangeably, contrast them directly: fifty = 5 tens; fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones. Say them slowly, stressing -ty vs -teen, and pair each with its base-ten model.
If reading 76 drifts toward a teen word, re-anchor on the tens: seventy is 7 tens, then the ones word -six follows, giving seventy-six.
activities.rationale: The -teen/-ty confusion is a persistent difficulty noted in teaching guidance; attaching each word to its numeral and a concrete quantity disambiguates by meaning. A listen-and-repeat prompt (optional tap-to-hear audio) can help learners hear the ending difference.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Take a minimal pair such as fifteen/fifty and read both aloud, stressing the ending (-teen vs -ty).
Beside each word, write its numeral (fifteen = 15, fifty = 50) and show a matching quantity or base-ten model (fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones; fifty = 5 tens).
Repeat with thirteen/thirty and other pairs, each time pairing word, numeral and quantity so meaning separates the near-identical sounds.
Answer a quick 'fifteen or fifty?' decision with the set of objects visible, choosing by quantity rather than guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: The '-ty' word names a number of tens (fifty = 5 tens) while the '-teen' word is a teen (fifteen = 1 ten and 5); linking each to a quantity removes the guesswork from the near-identical sounds.

activities.title: Use number words in a real read-and-write task
feedback: If the numeral comes out as 803 (or similarly 507 for fifty-seven), name the error (concatenating the spoken parts as full digits) and rebuild using a tens/ones frame so the ones digit sits in the ones place.
If teen and decade are swapped, return to the contrast pair with quantities before retrying.
Confirm success when the learner produces both directions correctly: 'seventy-six' for 76 and 83 for 'eighty-three'.
activities.rationale: Using the words in a live read/write task, rather than defining them, surfaces the specific slips (teen/decade confusion and the concatenation error) and shows real fluency across both directions. A short matching or fill-the-blank set (e.g. match 'seventy-two' to 72, spell the word for 45) consolidates afterward but checks recognition rather than independent production.
learnerActions: Given a label showing the numeral 76, write the words for a new label a customer could read ('seventy-six'), ordered correctly and hyphenated.
Given the word 'eighty-three' on a card, read it and write the numeral (83).
Check a friend's work: they wrote 803 for 'eighty-three' — decide whether it is right and explain what went wrong.
Compare 40 and 14 (and 'ninety' vs 'nineteen'): read each aloud and write each the other way to confirm you can move both directions.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has the system can move fluently in both directions — word to numeral and numeral to word — without concatenating the spoken parts or confusing teen and decade words.

constraints: Teach the decade words (twenty…ninety) as a set linked to the tens digit before drilling compounds, so compounds are built on an understood base.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity; spelling practice alone does not guarantee the words carry meaning.

Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds, and the commonly misspelled decade words forty (irregular: drops the u of four, not 'fourty') and ninety (regular: keeps the e of nine, not 'ninty'); coordinate with spelling/handwriting teaching.

Matching provided words to numerals checks recognition; independent spelling requires a response in which the word is not supplied. A free-writing or open fill-in task can elicit that production, especially when the learner also explains its quantity.

A static decade-word chart with tap-to-hear audio is a useful reference wall but does not rehearse active spelling/production or sound-alike discrimination; treat it as support, not the main practice.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Reading and writing numbers to 120
topic.description: Count to 120 starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals to 120
evidence: Count from 47 to 120 without errors
Read the numeral 108 correctly
Write the numeral for one hundred and fifteen
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} start counting from any number up to 120 — for example, starting at 87 and counting up to 120 without losing track?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7: count to 120 starting at ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120 — pushing counting and numeral fluency just past the 100 boundary into early three-digit territory.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number' (Y1); the to-120 extension mirrors the US Grade 1 expectation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120, starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral'.
• Operational details — two things matter: (i) counting on from any starting number (not always from 1), which shows counting is a movable sequence, and (ii) crossing 100 — reading/writing 100–120 (one hundred and eight = 108), where the hundreds place appears and children must not write 'one hundred and eight' as 1008. Rests on secure numerals to 100 and rote counting.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): count from 47 to 120 without error. Tier B (6–7): read the numeral 108 correctly. Tier C (7): write the numeral for 'one hundred and fifteen' (115), not 10015 or 1015.
bestPractices: Practise counting on FROM ANY number (start at 47, at 96, at 112) so children internalise that the count sequence can be entered anywhere — not a fixed chant from 1.
Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and the 100–120 numerals, where the new hundreds place trips reading/writing.
Confront the write-what-you-hear trap for three-digit words: 'one hundred and eight' → 108, NOT 1008; use place-value/arrow cards (100 + 8) to show the zero tens placeholder.
Extend the 100-square to a 120-grid so the pattern continues visibly past 100 and children see 101–120 as 'one hundred and ...'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary to build robust fluency.
keyRepresentations: 120-grid (extended 100-square) showing the pattern continuing past 100.
Bead string / number line to 120 for counting on from any point and crossing 100.
Place-value / arrow cards composing 108 as 100 + 8 (zero-tens placeholder visible).
Number track segments across the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Writing three-digit words literally: 'one hundred and eight' → 1008, or 'one hundred and fifteen' → 10015/1015 (missing the zero-tens placeholder or concatenating).
Stalling or resetting at 100 (saying 'one hundred, two hundred' or restarting at 1) when counting on.
Only being able to count from 1, not from an arbitrary start number.
Boundary slips: 99→'nine hundred' or 109→200-type errors.
Reading 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: count to 120 starting from ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120. Two skills carry the load: (i) counting on from an arbitrary start (not always from 1), so children feel the count as a movable sequence they can enter anywhere; and (ii) crossing 100 — reading and writing 100–120, where the hundreds place appears and children must learn that 'one hundred and eight' is 108, not 1008. Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and to the write-what-you-hear trap. The primary approach is an interactive 120-grid twinned with a number line; a static grid and short written/spoken checks are useful supporting tools with their own limits.

activities.title: Count on from any number across 100 (interactive grid and line)
feedback: If the count breaks at 99→100 or 109→110, don't reteach the whole sequence — rehearse just that boundary on a short track around it: 99, 100, 101 and 108, 109, 110.
If the child restarts at 1 or stalls at 100, nudge exactly at the boundary and model continuing: 'ninety-nine, one hundred, one hundred and one'.
If the child says 'nine hundred' after 99 or jumps to 200, point back to the grid so the next cell is visibly 100, then 101.
activities.rationale: Counting on from any number and crossing 100 are the known difficulty points for this age; rehearsing the exact boundary where errors cluster, with the sequence advancing visibly, is intended to build robust fluency. An interactive grid/line lets the child count, see the sequence advance, and get feedback at the boundary; a highlight-as-you-go display and a count-back mode make the mechanism concrete without being required.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
learnerActions: Pick any starting number — for example 47, 96, or 112 — and count on out loud, one number at a time, as each number is highlighted in turn on a 120-grid and a matching number line.

Deliberately practise starts that sit just before a boundary (start at 96 and count 97, 98, 99, 100, 101; start at 108 and count 109, 110, 111) so the century and decade rollovers get extra rehearsal.
Count backwards too (for example from 112 down past 100) to show the sequence runs both ways across the boundary.
While counting, keep the single running count going — avoid resetting to 1 or jumping to 'two hundred' after 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The count is a movable window you can enter at any number, not a fixed chant that must start at 1; it continues smoothly past 100, where 101–120 are 'one hundred and ...'.

activities.title: Build the numeral from the spoken words with place-value cards
feedback: If the child writes 1008 for 108 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, build the number with a hundred, tens and ones and write it into a hundreds/tens/ones frame; the 0 in 108 marks the empty tens.
If the child reads 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning, point to the hundred card and reread 'one hundred and eight'.
When a written numeral like 1008 is 'too long', compare it to the 120-grid to show it would land far off the board.
activities.rationale: The literal 'write what you hear' error is a specific, documented misconception for three-digit words; making the zero-tens placeholder visible through arrow/place-value cards is intended to directly address how the numeral is composed. Rejecting 1008 by showing it lands off a 120-grid is an optional feedback device that makes the error visible, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'one hundred and eight' and build it with place-value / arrow cards: pull the '100' card, note there are zero tens, then the '8' card, so the cards overlay to read 108.
Say what job the 0 is doing in 108 — it holds the empty tens place.
Do the same for 'one hundred and fifteen' → compose 100, then 1 ten, then 5, reading 115.
Confront the trap directly: write the words out literally (1008, 10015) and compare that number to where it would sit relative to the 120-grid — far off the board — to see why it can't be right.
activities.intendedInsight: Three-digit numerals are built by place value, not by stringing the spoken words together; the zero in 108 is a tens placeholder, and concatenating words gives numbers far too large.

activities.title: Fluency and trap checks: sequence, read, and write across 100
feedback: If a written answer is 1015 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, revisit the place-value build: 100, then 1 ten, then 5 → 115.
If a sequence answer breaks at 99→100, rehearse just that short run on a number line.
Confirm correct responses by rereading the numeral with its hundred meaning (108 = 'one hundred and eight').
activities.rationale: Short checks over sequence-filling, reading and words-to-numeral writing surface both the rollover stall and the concatenation error. These response formats are useful for checking fluency; note that choosing or completing an answer checks recognition and recall more than it elicits sustained independent counting, so pair it with the counting activity.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
learnerActions: Fill the missing numbers in a run that crosses the boundary, e.g. 97, 98, __, __, 101.
Read a given numeral aloud, e.g. 108, as 'one hundred and eight'.
Write the numeral for a spoken/written number word, e.g. 'one hundred and fifteen' → 115.
Use a slider or marker to land on target numbers up to 120.
activities.intendedInsight: These checks show whether a learner can complete sequences across 100, read numerals 100–120 with their hundred meaning, and write them by place value rather than concatenating words; sustained counting across 100 is confirmed through the spoken counting activity.

activities.title: 120-grid as a reference map
feedback: If a child is unsure what follows 99 or 109, locate it on the grid and read the next cell.
Reinforce that the two rows above 100 repeat the pattern of the first two rows: 101–110 matches 1–10, and 111–120 matches 11–20, with 'one hundred and ...' in front.
activities.rationale: A static 120-grid is a valuable reference that makes the continuing pattern visible, which supports the extension past 100. On its own a fixed grid does not rehearse the productive skills of counting on and writing numerals, so use it alongside counting and composing activities rather than as the main vehicle.
learnerActions: Explore a 120-grid, tapping cells to hear and see each numeral, with 101–120 displayed as 'one hundred and ...'.
Trace the pattern down each column and across each row to see how the sequence continues past 100 just as it did below it.
Point to where 99, 100, 109 and 110 sit and name them.
activities.intendedInsight: The counting pattern continues unbroken past 100, and 101–120 keep the same ones/tens pattern with 'one hundred and ...' in front.

constraints: Rests on secure numerals to 100 and secure rote counting; if counting across 100 fails, check these prerequisites first.
Give deliberate extra practice at the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and across 100–120, where reading/writing most often breaks.
A static 120-grid is a reference scaffold: it shows the pattern but does not itself let a child rehearse counting on or writing numerals, which are productive skills.
Choosing or completing answers checks recognition and recall; it does not by itself demonstrate sustained independent counting, so include spoken/written counting over a run that crosses 100.
Keep a single running count across the boundary — watch for resetting to 1, stalling at 100, or jumping to 'two hundred'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary.
Checkpoints: count from 47 to 120 without error (age 6); read 108 correctly (6–7); write 115 for 'one hundred and fifteen', not 10015 or 1015 (age 7).

activities.title: The 100-square vertical jump
feedback: If the child moves diagonally or sideways, point out that +10/-10 keeps the SAME column — only the row changes.

If the child moves in the wrong direction, link 'more' to the direction in which the numbers get bigger (down the grid on a top-down 100-square) and 'less' to the direction in which they get smaller (up).
Ask the child to compare the ones digit before and after: it should be identical every time.
When the child traces the vertical stripe, highlight that the move looks the same for every jump, which is why the shortcut always works.
activities.rationale: The 100-square's vertical structure makes 'ones unchanged, tens ±1' directly visible, so the child can see the pattern rather than memorise it. An optional interactive version — tap a number, press +10/-10, the highlight slides one row and the ones digit locks/glows while the tens digit ticks — may make the mechanism concrete, but a paper 100-square with a finger works for the move itself.

learnerActions: Point to a starting number on a 100-square (for example 56).

On a 100-square numbered from the top (1-10 in the top row), to find 10 more, move straight DOWN exactly one row, staying in the same column; to find 10 less, move straight UP one row in the same column. (On a bottom-up 100-square the directions are reversed. Check which way the numbers grow on your grid.)
Say the new number aloud (56 → 66 for 10 more, 56 → 46 for 10 less).
Repeat the +10 jump several times to trace a straight vertical stripe down the grid: 56 → 66 → 76 → 86.
Each time, name the ones digit and the tens digit and state what changed: 'the ones stayed 6, the tens went up by one.'
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten is always the same move — straight down or up one row — and the ones digit never moves because only a whole ten is added or removed.

activities.title: Add or remove one ten-rod
feedback: If the child disturbs the cubes, reset and emphasise that only a rod is added or removed.

activities.rationale: Physically adding/removing a single rod narrates the place-value reason the ones stay put, reinforcing the 100-square move with a different, hands-on representation. topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that ten single objects bundled together make 'one ten' — and that this is why we write 10 with a 1 in the tens place and a 0 in the ones place?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (CONCEPTUAL): understand that 10 can be thought of as a single BUNDLE of ten ones — a 'ten' — and that ten ones can be exchanged for one ten and back. This unitising move (centrality 0.41) is the bedrock of the entire base-ten system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones); non-statutory guidance on grouping in tens.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2a '10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a ten'.
• Operational details — the child physically groups ten single cubes into one tens-rod, and reverses it (exchange one ten for ten ones), grasping that '1 ten' and '10 ones' are the SAME quantity named/organised differently. This is UNITISING: treating a group as one thing while knowing it contains ten. It follows teen composition and precedes all multi-digit place value, comparison and column arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why. Tier B (6–7): explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten. Tier C (7): exchange 10 ones for a single tens block (and vice versa) fluently, using it in a simple problem.
bestPractices: Make the EXCHANGE physical and two-way: swap ten loose ones for one tens-rod and back, so children feel that regrouping conserves quantity — the ten IS ten ones, just bundled.
Use materials that show the ten is made of ten (a rod visibly ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar) BEFORE pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.
Name the unit deliberately — 'one ten' — and contrast counting 'ten ones' vs counting 'one ten' for the same pile, surfacing the unitising idea.
Link to the teens (prerequisite): a teen number already has one such bundle; now generalise the bundle itself as a countable unit toward decade numbers and two-digit place value.
Foreshadow regrouping in arithmetic: this exchange is exactly the 'carry/borrow' move children will meet in column addition and subtraction.
keyRepresentations: Ten single cubes physically snapping into one tens-rod (and the reverse).
Ten-bead bar / bead string where the ten is one strung unit of ten beads.
Exchange mat: 'ones' column and 'tens' column with a swap action (10 ones ↔ 1 ten).
Ten-frame filled completely = 'one ten' label.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

learn.summary: For children aged 6–7, build the concept that 10 ones can be bundled into a single 'ten' and exchanged back again, with the quantity conserved across the swap. This unitising move — treating a group of ten as one countable thing while knowing it still contains ten — is the foundation of base-ten place value, comparison and column arithmetic. The central activity is a two-way physical/interactive exchange with proportional materials (a rod visibly made of ten cubes) and deliberate naming of the same pile as 'ten ones' or 'one ten'. Supporting activities anchor the equivalence with a reveal, probe reasoning through dialogue, and check retention.

activities.title: Base-ten exchange: bundle and break a ten
feedback: If the child calls a rod 'one', break it apart in front of them and count the ten cubes, then rebuild it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.'
If the child thinks the rearranged amount changed, do it reversibly — build, break, rebuild — counting each time and stressing nothing was added or taken away.
Confirm success when the child exchanges both directions without recounting and names the same pile as either 'ten ones' or 'one ten'.
activities.rationale: Unitising is a physical bundling/exchange action; performing the two-way swap with proportional material lets conservation be felt and directly confronts the 'a rod is one' error. Proportional materials where the ten is visibly ten should precede pre-grouped abstract tokens so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.

Unitising — treating a bundle of ten as a single countable unit while knowing it contains ten ones — is the foundational concept of base-ten place value, best built with proportional materials and physical exchange.
learnerActions: Gather ten loose single cubes and join them into one tens-rod that is visibly ten cubes long.
Reverse the move: break (or separate) one tens-rod back into ten loose ones.
Watch or track a running count of the total cubes before and after each swap, and confirm it does not change.
Toggle/say the name for the very same pile two ways: 'ten ones' and 'one ten'.
Respond to challenges such as 'make one ten' and 'break a ten into ten ones, then give me 3 of them — how many loose ones are left?'
activities.intendedInsight: One ten and ten ones are the same quantity, named and organised two ways; bundling or unbundling changes the arrangement, not the amount, and the ten is itself a countable unit.

activities.title: Reveal the ten inside the rod
feedback: If the child guesses a number other than ten, count the revealed cubes together one by one.

activities.title: Prove it to the doubter
feedback: Accept the full explanation 'they are the same — the stick is ten ones bundled into one ten, so joining them doesn't change how many cubes there are.'

activities.rationale: Dialogue can surface and probe the unitising idea and distinguish 'equal because I counted' from 'equal because a ten IS ten ones'. Efficacy of the dialogue medium is not established by the cited sources, so it is proposed as a probe best paired with materials, so the child can act out the proof rather than only assert it.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who claims 'three rods is just three' or 'the loose pile is more than the stick'.
Explain and, if possible, demonstrate why one ten equals ten ones.

activities.title: Check the ten-ones equivalence
feedback: For a wrong value, return to the reveal or exchange activity and recount the ten.
Correct answer is ten ones.
activities.rationale: Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items are useful for checking whether the equivalence has stuck. Recognition items check retention; they do not elicit the independent bundling and exchange that builds the concept, so use them after hands-on work.

constraints: Use proportional materials where the ten is visibly made of ten (a rod ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar, a filled ten-frame) before introducing pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the tenness is seen not asserted.

The reveal image and the recognition quiz are scaffolds/checks: they anchor or test the equivalence but do not let the child perform the conserving exchange that builds unitising.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Break the stick apart in front of them and count 10; rebuild it. Name it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.' Use exchange games (10 ones ⇄ 1 ten).

sources.claim: Unitising — treating a bundle of ten as a single countable unit while knowing it contains ten ones — is the foundational concept of base-ten place value, best built with proportional materials and physical exchange.

representations: Ten single cubes physically snapping into one tens-rod (and the reverse).
Ten-bead bar / bead string where the ten is one strung unit of ten beads.

constraints: Use proportional materials where the ten is visibly made of ten (a rod ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar, a filled ten-frame) before introducing pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the tenness is seen not asserted.
Make the exchange genuinely two-way: bundling ten ones into a ten AND breaking a ten back into ten ones; reversing the bundle is the move needed later for borrowing in subtraction.
Name the unit deliberately as 'one ten' and contrast counting 'ten ones' versus 'one ten' for the same pile.
The reveal image and the recognition quiz are scaffolds/checks: they anchor or test the equivalence but do not let the child perform the conserving exchange that builds unitising.

misconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} the numbers 34, 67, and 21, can they put them in order from smallest to largest — and use the symbols > or < correctly?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Compare and order two-digit numbers using >, =, < based on PLACE VALUE: compare the tens first, and only if the tens are equal compare the ones. A procedural skill built directly on tens-and-ones understanding.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100; use <, > and = signs'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.3 'compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results with the symbols >, =, and <'.
• Operational details — Establish the meaning of each symbol before speed ('the open mouth eats the bigger number' is a crutch; ground it in 'greater than/less than' with quantities). Teach the leading-digit rule explicitly: compare tens, decide; if tens tie, compare ones. Use base-ten blocks or a number line so 'bigger' is a seen quantity/position, not a guess. Progress from comparing pairs to ordering a set (smallest→largest and largest→smallest).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): place > or < between two numbers with clearly different tens (34, 52) and justify by the tens. Tier B (age 6-7): compare a same-tens pair (34, 38) by the ones and place the correct symbol. Tier C (age 7): order a mixed set of five two-digit numbers and explain the tens-then-ones rule, including a same-tens tie.
bestPractices: Compare quantities and positions FIRST (blocks side by side, points on a 0-100 line) so 'greater' means visibly more, then attach the symbol — symbol before meaning breeds the crocodile-mouth-without-understanding error.
Teach the leading-digit strategy explicitly: look at the tens; the number with more tens is greater; only if the tens are equal do you compare the ones.
Read the statement both ways — 34 < 43 as 'thirty-four is less than forty-three' AND 43 > 34 — so the child sees the relation is the same fact stated from either end.
Use same-tens pairs (34 vs 38) deliberately to force attention onto the ones once tens are equal, defeating 'just compare the first digit'.
Move from pairwise comparison to ordering a set, recording with symbols, so comparison becomes a tool for organising numbers, not an isolated trick.

0-100 number line where the number further right is greater
Tens|ones place-value chart aligning two numbers column by column
The <, >, = symbols with the 'points to the smaller / opens to the larger' orientation, grounded in quantity
Ordered track or 'washing line' for pegging a set of numbers smallest to largest
commonMisconceptions: Using the crocodile/Pac-Man mouth as a rote trick with no sense of which number is actually bigger, so the symbol is placed by guess.
Comparing by digit count of the numeral or by the ONES first (34 vs 38: choosing by 4 vs 8 alone is fine here, but 52 vs 48 wrongly judged by 2 vs 8) — ignoring the leading (tens) digit.
Reversing the symbol — knowing which is bigger but writing > where < belongs.
Thinking = can only sit between identical-looking expressions, not that it asserts equal value.
For same-tens pairs, defaulting to 'they're the same' because the tens match, instead of moving to the ones.

activities.title: Comparison bench: build, see, and place the symbol
feedback: If the symbol is placed correctly, confirm by showing the greater pile 'winning' or the line marker leaning toward the larger number: the wide open side faces the larger number, the point faces the smaller.

If the symbol is reversed but the reasoning is right ('43 is bigger' yet < is written), separate the two steps: praise the correct comparison, then re-anchor the orientation — open side toward the larger number — and have them re-read the whole statement aloud to check.
If 'greater' is guessed from the numeral shape (e.g. 'longer looks bigger'), return to the blocks/line so 'greater' is a seen quantity, then re-attach the symbol.
activities.rationale: Comparison becomes meaningful when two quantities are shown as blocks and as points on a line before a symbol is attached, so 'greater' is visibly more rather than a guess. Showing both forms and reading the statement both ways grounds the symbols in quantity and treats the relation as a single reversible fact. An optional live version (dragging the symbol into the gap with the greater pile lighting up and the line marker leaning) makes the mechanism concrete, but the core learning works with physical blocks and a drawn line.

learnerActions: Build or show two two-digit numbers in two forms at once: base-ten block piles and dots/markers on a shared 0-100 number line.

Decide which is greater by looking at the quantity/position first (more tens rods and more blocks in total, further right on the line), then say it aloud: e.g. 'forty-three is greater than thirty-four'.
Place the correct symbol (<, >, or =) into the gap between the two numbers.
Read the completed statement both ways: 34 < 43 ('thirty-four is less than forty-three') and 43 > 34 ('forty-three is greater than thirty-four').
State the rule used: compare the tens first; the number with more tens is greater, and if the tens are equal, compare the ones.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Greater' and 'less' name a real difference in quantity/position, and the symbol records that relation — the same fact can be read from either end.

activities.title: Tens-tie rounds: when the first digit can't decide
feedback: If the child says a same-tens pair is 'the same' because the tens match, prompt them to move on to the ones: 3 tens and 4 ones versus 3 tens and 8 ones.
For 52 vs 48, if the child picks 48 as larger because 8 > 2, rebuild both with tens and ones so that five tens clearly outweigh four tens; the ones only matter once the tens tie.
For 60 and 60, if the child hesitates to use =, confirm that = means equal value and both quantities match exactly.
activities.rationale: Same-tens pairs deliberately force attention onto the ones once the tens are equal, defeating the 'just compare the first digit' error; crossed-decade pairs (e.g. 52 vs 48) expose the ones-first misconception directly. An optional auto-generated 'tens tie' mode makes these cases frequent, but a teacher-chosen set of pairs serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Grounding comparison symbols in quantity/position and teaching a tens-then-ones leading-digit strategy prevents rote crocodile-mouth errors.
1.NBT.3: compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording with >, =, <.
learnerActions: Compare same-tens pairs such as 34 and 38, where the tens columns are identical.
Notice that the tens no longer settle it, then compare the ones to decide which is greater.
Place the correct symbol and justify: 'the tens are the same, so I looked at the ones'.
Try a 'crossed-decade' pair such as 52 and 48, and check: 52 has more tens, so it is greater even though its ones digit (2) is smaller than 8.
Also handle an equal pair such as 60 and 60, choosing = and explaining that both show the same value.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing only the first digit you see is not enough: compare the tens first, and only when the tens are equal does the ones digit decide. = asserts equal value, not merely identical-looking symbols.

activities.title: Order a scrambled set onto a washing line
feedback: If a number with a large ones digit is placed too high (e.g. 19 above 51), rebuild both with blocks so 51's five tens stand against 19's single ten, then re-place.
If ordering is correct one way but shaky the other, have the child read the finished line aloud in both directions to confirm it is the same facts reversed.
Confirm a correct order by checking each neighbouring pair with a symbol.
activities.rationale: Moving from pairwise comparison to ordering a set, recording with symbols, makes comparison a practical tool and surfaces whether tens genuinely govern the child's decisions. An ordering mode where numbers are dragged onto a washing line and checked left-to-right is one concrete way to do this; pegged cards on a string work equally well.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of two-digit numbers, e.g. 19, 27, 51, 72, and arrange them smallest to largest.
Repeat, ordering the same set largest to smallest.
Include a set containing a same-tens tie so ordering requires the ones to break it.
Check the finished order left to right and record the relations with symbols where appropriate.
Explain how you decided the order: tens first across the set, ones to break ties.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison is a tool for organising numbers: ordering a set applies the tens-then-ones rule repeatedly, not as an isolated trick.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how do you know?'
feedback: If the child explains correctly but writes the symbol backwards, treat orientation as a separate, fixable step and re-read the statement aloud.
If the child cannot say why the tens were examined first, return to blocks to re-establish that a ten is worth more than a one.
activities.rationale: A short Socratic probe on a tricky same-tens or crossed-decade pair may elicit and correct compare-the-tens-first reasoning and catch the ones-first error. Talking out the reasoning complements the hands-on and symbol-placing practice; it is offered alongside that work rather than as a substitute for it.
sourceClaims: Grounding comparison symbols in quantity/position and teaching a tens-then-ones leading-digit strategy prevents rote crocodile-mouth errors.
learnerActions: Explain aloud which digit you looked at first and why, on a tricky pair such as 52 and 48.
Answer: '34 and 43 use the same two digits — how can one be bigger?' by referring to place value.
Decide and justify the symbol for an equal pair like 60 and 60.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a comparison out loud reveals and corrects the reasoning (tens first, ones to break a tie) behind the written symbol.

activities.title: Consolidation and check: choose, order, fill the gap
feedback: For a wrong symbol, ask the child to identify which is greater first, then fix the orientation separately.
For a mis-ordered set, direct attention to the tens across the whole set before the ones.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering map cleanly onto choose-the-symbol, order-the-set, and fill-the-gap tasks, making this a natural consolidation and check surface. These tasks drill and check the skill; on their own they do not build the underlying quantity sense, so they should follow the block/line and tens-tie work rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Choose the correct symbol between two numbers, including a same-tens item and an item designed to tempt symbol reversal.
Order a scrambled set smallest to largest.
Fill in the missing symbol in a statement and read it back aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: The tens-then-ones comparison and correct symbol use can be applied quickly and reliably across varied pairs and sets.

constraints: Establish the meaning of each symbol with quantities/positions before pushing for speed; 'the open mouth eats the bigger number' is only a memory crutch and must be grounded in 'greater than / less than' with real quantities.
Treat recognition and drill tasks (choosing or filling a symbol) as consolidation/check; they verify the skill but do not by themselves build quantity sense or independent reasoning.

A single fixed illustration can anchor the tens-then-ones rule with one worked pair, but on its own it cannot let the child compare varied pairs or order a set, which is where the skill is practised; use it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Keep symbol orientation (open side to the larger number) as a separate check from the greater/less reasoning, so a correct comparison written with a reversed symbol is diagnosed accurately.
Base-ten blocks and the drawn number line are physical representations with slight thickness; they stand for the abstract numerical values being compared, not the values themselves.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted CCSS alignment as 1.NBT.3 (Grade 1) while targeting UK Y2 (ages 6-7); the standards citations are from different jurisdictions/grades and were preserved as written, not independently reconfirmed.

topic.name: Place value understanding and number facts
topic.description: Use place value understanding and number facts to solve problems
evidence: Use knowledge that 34 = 30 + 4 to help add 34 + 20 = 54
Solve 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45. What was my number?'
Apply partitioning to solve a problem in an unfamiliar context
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked 'which number is closest to 50 — 47 or 54?', can they use their number knowledge to answer quickly and explain why?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), META. Use place-value understanding AND known number facts together to solve problems: knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and a bond like 3+2=5 lets you reason 34 + 20 = 54, or work backwards ('add 10 to my number and I get 45'). This is the application layer that turns tens-and-ones knowledge into a problem-solving tool.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'use place value and number facts to solve problems'; recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4/5/6 and 2.NBT.5–9 — add/subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations; mentally find 10 more/less.
• Operational details — Keep it strategy-based, not algorithm-based at this stage: partition (34 = 30 + 4), operate on the parts, recombine. Model missing-number and 'I think of a number' problems that demand working backwards. Emphasise that a known fact (3+2) plus place value (these are TENS) generates a new fact (30+20). Use concrete/pictorial support and expect children to explain WHICH fact and WHICH partition they used.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use 34 = 30 + 4 to add a multiple of ten (34 + 20) with blocks. Tier B (age 6-7): solve a one-step missing-number problem ('__ + 10 = 45') by reasoning about the tens. Tier C (age 7): solve a two-step or unfamiliar-context problem, choosing a partition and a known fact, and explain the reasoning.
bestPractices: Teach partition–operate–recombine explicitly: split into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, put it back together — making the place-value structure the engine of the strategy.
Connect a known bond to its place-value scaling out loud: 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50' — so number facts and place value are used together, not in isolation.
Use missing-number and 'think of a number' problems to force flexible, backwards reasoning rather than one-directional calculation.
Insist on explanation/justification ('which fact did you use? how did you split it?') so the META goal — choosing and applying structure — is assessed, not just the answer.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram splitting a number into tens and ones
Base-ten blocks for partition–operate–recombine
Empty/marked number line for jumps of tens and ones
Bar model for missing-number and comparison problems
Fact-family / derived-fact chains (3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54)
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a counting-in-ones or column method instead of using place-value structure, because the number-fact link was never made.
Applying a known bond but forgetting the unit — saying 30 + 20 = 5 (using 3+2 but dropping the tens).
Unable to work backwards — treating 'think of a number' problems as if they can only be solved forwards.
Partitioning incorrectly under a problem's wording (mis-splitting 34 as 3 + 4 rather than 30 + 4).
Focusing on getting an answer without checking it fits the problem, so an unreasonable result goes unquestioned.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2), help children use place-value structure together with known number facts to solve problems — e.g. knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and 3 + 2 = 5 to reason that 34 + 20 = 54, and to work backwards on 'I think of a number' problems. The core strategy is partition–operate–recombine: split a number into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, then put it back together, saying aloud which fact and which partition were used. Keep it strategy-based (not column algorithm) at this stage, support with concrete and pictorial models, and insist on explanation so the META goal — choosing and justifying structure — is what develops.

activities.title: Problem playground: partition, operate, recombine
feedback: If the child counts all 54 from one, prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' and show the shortcut (30 + 20) beside the count rather than reteaching the bonds.

If the child refuses to attempt because 'we haven't done this one', think aloud how a known fact generates a new one, name derivation as real mathematics, and invite them to build the next step themselves.
If they say 30 + 20 = 5, point back to the blocks: these are tens, so the answer is 50, not 5 — the unit must be kept.
If they split 34 as 3 + 4, re-anchor on the part-whole diagram: the 3 stands for 30 (three tens).
For the work-backwards mode, if they treat it as only solvable forwards, invite them to test a value and check whether '+10' lands on 45, adjusting up or down.
activities.rationale: Making partition–operate–recombine visible and generative lets the place-value structure act as the engine of the strategy; auto-generating fresh problems supports transfer, and a work-backwards mode forces flexible reasoning. Linked fact-chains and live recombination (e.g. a fact ribbon lighting up, number-line testing) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Take a problem such as 34 + 20 and split 34 into a 30-part and a 4-part (using base-ten blocks, a part-whole 'cherry' diagram, or drawing).
Add the 20 onto the tens part only, saying aloud 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50'.
Recombine the parts: 50 + 4 = 54, and state the full chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54.
Try a 'mystery number' / work-backwards problem such as '__ + 10 = 45': cover or guess the start number and test candidate values on a number line until the equation holds.
Repeat with fresh problems (e.g. 34 + 30, 56 + 20) so the strategy — not one answer — is what transfers.
activities.intendedInsight: A number bond you already own (like 3 + 2) can do the heavy lifting on tens, so an unfamiliar calculation can be derived by partitioning and recruiting a known fact rather than counted out from one.

activities.title: Socratic coaching: which fact and which split?
feedback: If the child reverts to counting, nudge toward place value: 'what known fact is hiding in here?'
If they cannot say why splitting 34 into 30 and 4 is legitimate, revisit the part-whole model to show the whole is unchanged.
Affirm reasoning that names both the partition and the fact, even if the final arithmetic needs a small correction.
activities.rationale: Because this is a META skill about choosing and justifying, dialogue that asks the child to state and defend a method can develop the reasoning and respond to the child's chosen approach. This is offered as one effective format alongside hands-on work, not as the only way to teach justification.

learnerActions: Face a posed problem (e.g. 34 + 20 or a two-step unfamiliar-context problem) and explain the method you would choose before calculating.

Answer probes: 'What did you already know that you leaned on?', 'How could you use what you already know to solve this?', 'Which fact helped, and why?', 'Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4 — why doesn't that change the answer?'

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–8 (REPRESENTATIONAL): identify, represent and ESTIMATE numbers using different representations — objects, base-ten blocks, drawings, place-value charts and especially the NUMBER LINE — and move flexibly between them.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y3): 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line' (Y1), and 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations' (Y2, Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.MD.6 (number line as a measurement/position model), 1.NBT/2.NBT representations; the number line as a representation of magnitude runs throughout.
• Operational details — the core is REPRESENTATIONAL FLEXIBILITY: the same number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, or an expanded form, and the child translates between them. ESTIMATION on a number line (roughly where does 47 sit on 0–100? about how many in this pile?) develops magnitude/number sense, not just exact counting. The number line is the load-bearing representation — it encodes order AND relative size.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): place a two-digit number on a 0–100 line in roughly the right position. Tier B (7): represent the same number with base-ten blocks, a number line and a drawing; match a base-ten picture to its numeral. Tier C (7–8): estimate where a three-digit number falls on a 0–1000 line and estimate 'about how many' in a set without counting.
bestPractices: Deliberately represent the SAME number many ways (set, base-ten blocks, number line point, numeral, expanded form) and have children translate between them — representational flexibility, not one favourite model, is the goal.

Use the number line as the anchor representation for MAGNITUDE and estimation: 'about where does 47 go?' builds the sense that numbers have relative size and order, feeding later rounding and decimals.
Teach estimation as a valued skill in its own right ('about how many', 'roughly where') with landmarks/benchmarks (0, 50, 100; halfway) rather than treating every task as exact counting.
Use empty/partially-marked number lines so children reason from benchmarks rather than counting every interval — a key step toward proportional placement.
Connect base-ten-block representations to the place-value the blocks encode (tens rods, ones cubes) so 'representing' reinforces, not bypasses, place value.

Placing numbers on a line by counting marks only, ignoring proportional spacing (47 put just past 0, or bunched near a benchmark).

activities.title: Many faces of the same number
feedback: If a child can build 34 with blocks but not place it on a line, pause on translating just those two forms: build 34, then point to roughly where it sits and check they agree.
When blocks and numeral disagree, ask them to recount by tens and ones (rods then cubes) rather than counting every single cube.
Praise correct translations by naming the link: 'Three tens-rods and four cubes IS 34 IS 30 + 4.'

If an interactive linker is available, the optional live cross-updating (change the numeral and watch the blocks, expanded form and line point shift together) makes the 'same number' idea visible; a tap-to-reveal poster showing one number five ways is a lower-tech alternative.
activities.rationale: Representational flexibility — translating the same number across forms, not favouring one model — is the core objective at this stage, and connecting base-ten blocks to the tens/ones they encode keeps representation tied to place value.
sourceClaims: Pupils identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line, and identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations.
learnerActions: Pick a number (e.g. 247) and build it several ways: a set or base-ten blocks (2 hundreds flats, 4 tens rods, 7 ones cubes), the numeral 247, the expanded form 200 + 40 + 7, and words.
Place that same number as a point on a number line.
Change one representation and update all the others to match so they always show the same quantity (e.g. add one tens rod to make 257, then fix the numeral, the expanded form and the line point).
Say aloud why these are all the 'same number wearing different clothes'.
Match a mixed set of base-ten pictures to their numerals and to the matching words.
activities.intendedInsight: A single number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, expanded form or words, and you can translate between them because they all encode the same quantity.

activities.title: Estimate on a benchmarked number line

Probe with: 'Where would 50 go? How do you know that's the middle?' and 'You placed 40 there — is it nearer 0 or nearer 100?'
Check consistency across representations: 'Show me 40 with base-ten blocks, then point to it on the line — do they agree?'
Check scale awareness: 'If the line went 0 to 1000 instead of 0 to 100, would 40 sit in the same place? Why not?'
A correct response reads the mark as about 70 by proportion (past the middle, most of the way to 100) and places 40 a little below the halfway point, using 0, 50 and 100 as benchmarks.

If a drag-and-drop estimation tool is available, an optional feedback band showing how close the placement is rewards proportional reasoning over mark-counting; the same judgement can be practised on paper with a pencil placement and a reveal of the true position.
activities.rationale: The number line carries both order and relative size, and benchmark-based placement rather than counting every mark develops magnitude sense that later supports rounding and decimals. activities.title: About how many? — estimating set size
feedback: If a child insists on counting every object, affirm that counting is useful but set a short time or hide the set so they must judge magnitude instead.
Encourage anchoring: 'This looks like about three groups of ten, so around thirty.'
Treat any estimate inside a reasonable band as a success and name the reasoning, not just the number.
activities.rationale: Some children believe estimation is 'wrong maths' and want to count exactly; teaching estimation as a skill in its own right, with benchmarks, builds number sense.
sourceClaims: Pupils identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line, and identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations.
learnerActions: Look at a pile or set of 30–50 objects for only a brief moment (too briefly to count every one).
Give a sensible estimate of 'about how many', and say what helped you judge (e.g. comparing to a known group of ten).
Compare your estimate to the actual count and reflect on how close it was.
Discuss that a good estimate within a sensible range is valuable maths, not 'wrong' because it is not exact.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating 'about how many' is a real, valued skill: judging magnitude quickly using benchmarks is different from, and complements, exact counting.

constraints: A tap-to-reveal poster or a static 'same number five ways' display is a useful reference for the links between representations, but on its own it does not give placement or estimation practice; pair it with actual line placement and 'about how many' tasks.

A slider or matching quiz (place a number on a line, match blocks to numeral, choose an estimate for a flashed set) is suitable for checking representational links and estimation, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a number across forms — include tasks where the child builds and translates representations.
Keep base-ten work tied to place value: children should read rods and flats as tens and hundreds, not count every unit cube.

Number lines used for placement and estimation must show their endpoints (e.g. 0–100 or 0–1000) and be drawn to a uniform scale, so equal distances stand for equal differences even where no interior marks are drawn; children should check whether the line runs to 100 or 1000. Open 'empty' number lines used for jottings are not drawn to scale, so do not use them for proportional estimation.

Early number-line estimates are commonly uneven: small numbers are spread too far apart and larger numbers are crowded together toward the upper end. Treat this as developmental and respond with benchmark practice, not by marking placements wrong.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30 … 90) each represent a whole number of TENS and ZERO ones: 30 means 3 tens and 0 ones. A special, high-frequency case of two-digit place value where the ones column is empty.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number, forward and backward'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2c 'the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones)'.
• Operational details — Build each decade with tens rods only (no unit cubes) and place them in the tens column with an explicit 0 written in the ones column, so the empty ones place is SEEN, not omitted. Tie to skip-counting in tens (10, 20, 30 …) so the spoken sequence and the tens count line up. Contrast a decade (40 = 4 tens, 0 ones) with a nearby non-decade (43 = 4 tens, 3 ones) to fix the role of the zero.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): skip-count 10, 20, 30 … 90 and build 30 with three rods. Tier B (age 6-7): say '30 is 3 tens and 0 ones' and write 30 = 30 + 0 / 3 tens. Tier C (age 7): match any decade to its tens representation and explain why the 0 is needed (place-holder in the ones).
bestPractices: Build decades with tens rods ONLY and write a 0 in the ones column so the child sees the ones place is filled by zero, not absent — this is the seed of the place-holder idea.
Anchor to skip-counting in tens on a bead string or number track so '3 tens' and 'thirty' and the third stop line up as the same thing.
Contrast a decade with an adjacent non-decade (40 vs 43) so the 0 earns its meaning as 'no ones', not 'nothing'.
Name the decade words carefully (thirty, forty, fifty) and connect the '-ty' to 'tens', flagging the thirteen/thirty and fifteen/fifty confusions.
Use the tens|ones chart to show that reading only the tens column gives the decade name — reinforcing column-based reading of two-digit numbers.

Bead string / number track marked in tens for skip-counting

activities.title: Building decades with tens rods and a visible zero
feedback: If the child says the 0 'means nothing', rebuild 30 with rods and no cubes and point to the empty ones spot: that empty spot IS the zero — zero ones. Contrast 3 and 30 to show the 0 keeps the 3 in the tens place (and, if ready, 300, where two zeros hold the 3 in the hundreds place) — zeros act as place-holders in their own place.
If the child reads the 3 at face value ('three'), count the ones inside the three rods (30) and say '3 in the tens place = 3 tens = 30'.
When the child adds the loose cube and 30 becomes 31, affirm: the 0 was doing real work holding the ones place empty; once a one is there, the ones digit reads 1.
Praise explanations that state both parts: '3 tens AND 0 ones'.
activities.rationale: Making the quantity drive the numeral while the zero is held visibly in place lets children connect the spoken sequence, the tens count, and the written form, and distinguishes a decade from a non-decade. learnerActions: Set up a tens|ones chart (drawn or physical) with two columns.

topic.name: The two digits of a two-digit number
topic.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 47, can they tell you there are 4 tens (forty) and 7 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'four seven'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of TENS and ONES: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. This is the central node of early place value — the tens/ones column idea that every later place-value column extends.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2 'understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones' with 1.NBT.2a/b/c; consolidated in 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Build every two-digit number CONCRETELY first (bundled tens + loose ones), then match to the written numeral and to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7). Insist the child reads the tens digit as a QUANTITY OF TENS, not the face value ('four tens', not 'four'). Contrast standard partition (47 = 40 + 7) with non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17) once secure, because flexible partitioning underpins later column addition/subtraction.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): with base-ten blocks present, build 47 and say '4 tens and 7 ones'. Tier B (age 6-7): given 47 with no blocks, state the value of each digit (40 and 7) and write 47 = 40 + 7. Tier C (age 7): identify the tens/ones digit in any two-digit number and give a non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17).
bestPractices: Follow the CPA sequence: bundle ten loose ones into a labelled 'ten' (concrete), draw it as a ten-rod/line (pictorial), then link to the numeral 47 and expanded form 40+7 (abstract) — never leave the digit floating free of a quantity.
Use a place-value chart with only two columns (tens | ones) and physically place bundled tens in the tens column and loose ones in the ones column so the position IS the meaning.
Read the digits by value out loud — '4 tens' and '7 ones' — and resist 'four, seven'; language that names the unit prevents the digits-are-just-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) deliberately once standard partitioning is secure, so children see the tens/ones split as flexible, not a single fixed answer.
Use 'the same number, many ways' tasks: show 47 as blocks, as 40+7, as a point on a 0-100 line, and as a bead string of 4 tens + 7 — same quantity, different representation.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (tens rods + unit cubes) — the canonical proportional model where a ten is physically ten ones
Two-column tens|ones place-value chart with bundled tens and loose ones placed in position
Expanded-form / part-whole (cherry) diagram: 47 splits into 40 and 7
Bead strings and ten-frames grouped into complete tens plus extras
Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7) that physically overlap to build 47, making expanded form tangible
commonMisconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2 / US Grade 1-2), build the understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for a quantity of tens and a quantity of ones: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Centre the learning on concrete grouping — bundling ten loose ones into one ten — then link that quantity to the written numeral, to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7), and to flexible (non-standard) partitioning (47 = 30 + 17). Read digits by value ('four tens', 'seven ones'), never as bare faces.

activities.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
feedback: If the child says 'the 4 means four', have them count the single cubes inside the four bundles: there are forty, so the 4 is worth 4 tens = 40.

If the child places tens in the ones column (or vice versa), name the columns again — tens on the left, ones on the right — and compare 47 with 74 built side by side so the positions are visibly different quantities.
When partitioning as 30 + 17, confirm by re-counting the whole pile: if it is still 47, the split is valid; the quantity is conserved even though the grouping changed.
If the child thinks a decade like 40 has 'nothing' in the ones, show 40 as four tens and zero loose ones — the ones place is still there, holding none.
activities.rationale: Place value is a quantity re-seen as grouped units. Acting out the bundling (ten ones fusing into one ten) makes unitising something the child does rather than a label they repeat, which is the standard concrete-first (CPA) route and is intended to target the face-value and concatenation errors.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.2 states the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones, with 10 as a bundle of ten ones.
Explicit CPA (concrete-pictorial-abstract) sequencing and standard/non-standard partitioning are recommended for building place-value understanding.
learnerActions: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
activities.intendedInsight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.

activities.title: Many ways to show the same number
feedback: If the child marks 47 near the wrong end of the line, count up in tens (10, 20, 30, 40) then on by ones to locate it.
For 44, if the child says both 4s mean the same, point to the place of each: the left 4 sits in the tens column (40), the right 4 in the ones column (4).
If the child drops the ones place for 40, have them state it as '4 tens and 0 ones' to keep the place visible.
If the arrow cards are read as '4' and '7', separate then re-overlap them so the '40' card is seen whole underneath the '7'.
activities.rationale: Linking multiple representations of one quantity is intended to build the flexible, connected understanding named in the Y2 standard, including representing numbers on a number line, and guards against treating each representation as a separate fact.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils should recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and identify/represent/estimate numbers using different representations including the number line.
learnerActions: Take one number, e.g. 47, and represent it several ways: as bundled tens + loose ones, as expanded form 40 + 7, as a part-whole (cherry) diagram with 47 at the top splitting into 40 and 7, as a point marked at 47 on a 0-100 number line, as a bead string of 4 tens plus 7 beads, and by overlapping arrow/place-value cards (a '40' card with a '7' card sliding over it to read 47).
Check that every representation is the same quantity by counting back to 47 each time.
Repeat with a decade number such as 40 and with a number containing a repeated digit such as 44, explaining why the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts (40 and 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is a single quantity that can be shown in many different ways; the tens/ones meaning stays the same across blocks, numerals, expanded form, the part-whole diagram, arrow cards, and the number line.

activities.title: Convince me the 4 means forty
feedback: Accept any justification that ties the digit to its place and counts the underlying ones (four tens = forty).
If the child only restates 'it's forty because it is', ask them to point to and count the actual tens to ground the claim.
Treat this as a short follow-up after concrete building, not a substitute for it — the child's reasoning can then be tied to bundles they have actually handled.
activities.rationale: A brief reasoning prompt may surface whether the child attaches the digit to its place or is reciting; it is proposed to work best as consolidation after hands-on grouping rather than as the first encounter, since the concept is grounded in manipulating quantities. Discussion alone can elicit an explanation but does not itself provide the physical grouping.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Convince me the 4 in 47 is worth forty, not four.'
Justify using a model you built — e.g. 'because the 4 is four bundles, and each bundle is ten, so that is forty.'
Extend to a prove-it task: 'Show that the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why a digit's value comes from its place cements the idea beyond stating the rule.

activities.title: Check and sort by place value
feedback: For a swap error, rebuild 47 and 74 side by side so the different tens counts are visible.
For 4 + 7 = 11, show that the digits are not added together; the 4 counts tens and the 7 counts ones, giving 40 + 7 = 47.
For 47 = 30 + ___, confirm the missing part is 17 by regrouping one ten into ten ones.
For 47 = ___ + 7, confirm the missing part is 40 (four tens).
activities.rationale: Targeted checks that include the two headline distractors (transposition, 74, and adding the digits at face value, 11) can confirm the idea is held and probe the specific misconceptions. A check or sort can classify and verify a child's answers but does not itself elicit the physical grouping, so pair it with the building activity.
learnerActions: Complete expanded-form blanks, e.g. 47 = ___ + 7 and 47 = 30 + ___.
Choose which picture shows 4 tens and 7 ones, and match written numerals to their block pictures.
Sort or state, for a given two-digit number, which digit is the tens digit and which is the ones digit, and the value of each.
Consider tempting wrong answers — e.g. 74 (digits swapped) and 11 (adding 4 + 7) — and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each digit's value is fixed by its place, and conscious rejection of the swap error (74) and the digit-adding/face-value error (11, from adding 4 + 7).

constraints: Always build a two-digit number concretely first (bundled tens + loose ones), then connect it to the numeral and expanded form; never leave a digit floating free of a quantity.
Read digits by unit aloud — 'four tens', 'seven ones' — not 'four, seven'; naming the unit prevents the digits-as-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) only once standard partitioning (47 = 40 + 7) is secure.
A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.

A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.

Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a group of 14 objects, can they tell you whether that number is odd or even — for example by pairing them up to see if any are left over?

pedagogy.summary:

Introduce the last-digit shortcut only AFTER the pairing meaning is secure, and justify it via the pairs in the ones.
