activities.title: Pair-them-up frame
feedback: If the learner thinks odd/even depends on the number being big or small, show a small odd number and a large even number side by side so size is decoupled from parity.
When a counter is stranded, highlight it (e.g. it glows or wobbles alone) and name it 'the leftover with no partner — that's what odd means'.
When the slider ticks up, prompt: 'Did adding one make a new pair, or leave one stranded? What does that make the number now?'
When a child writes 8 = 4 + 4, connect it to the frame: 'four pairs, or two equal groups of four — that's why it's even.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the pairing action, so letting the child change the count and watch the parity flip makes the alternating structure and the doubles link concrete. The live recolouring, lone-counter highlight, slider, and equal-addends strip are optional interaction examples that make the pairing mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).

learnerActions: Choose a number of counters (start up to 10, then up to 20) and drop them into a two-row frame so they arrange into pairs.
Look at the result: if one counter is left with no partner the number is ODD; if every counter is matched the number is EVEN.
Use a slider or counter to add one and remove one, watching whether the lone counter appears or disappears each time.
Say out loud what changes each step: adding one either strands a single counter (makes it odd) or creates a new pair (makes it even).
Use an 'equal addends' strip to write each even number as n + n (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is even when its objects pair with none left over and odd when exactly one is left over; because adding one either completes a pair or strands a single, odd and even alternate, and every even number is a double (n + n).

activities.title: Predict then check with real counters
feedback: If a child says 13 is even because 'you can split it into 7 and 6', have them line the 7 and 6 up in pairs and show that one is stranded — even means pairs with none left over, so the two groups must be equal.
If a child answers instantly from size ('even because it's big'), show small and large numbers of each parity so size is clearly not the rule.
If the reasoning is right ('one left over means odd') but the count slips, slow the one-to-one matching and recount the leftover pile — the concept is intact; support the counting.
For 0: there is nothing left unpaired, so 0 is even — invite the child to articulate this with the 'none left over' definition.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a stated reason exposes whether a child treats 'odd' as an unpairable leftover or just as a label, and separates conceptual misunderstanding (unequal-split or size rules) from simple miscounting.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a pile of counters (e.g. 13). Before touching them, predict whether they will all get a partner or whether one will be left over, and say why.
Pair them two-by-two to check your prediction.
Discuss: why is 13 odd but 12 even — what changes when you add one more?
Tackle a friend's claim that 'zero is odd because there's nothing to pair', and decide whether 0 is odd or even.
Try reasoning about a large number (e.g. 100 or 24 or 47): how could you tell odd or even without pairing every one?
activities.intendedInsight: Parity is about whether everything pairs with nothing left over, not about size or whether the number can be split into any two groups; this reasoning generalises to larger numbers.

activities.title: Counting in 2s and the last-digit rule

If skip-counting and pairing give different answers, recount together — both methods should agree for the same number.
Link each even result back to a double (n + n) to reinforce that even numbers are made of pairs.

constraints: Anchor the concept in the pairing action first; introduce the last-digit shortcut only after the pairing meaning is secure and have children justify it: every ten splits into 5 pairs with none left over, so only the ones can leave a leftover.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 10 or 100 More or Less
topic.description: Find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number up to 1000
evidence: Given a three-digit number, state what is 10 more and 10 less
Given a three-digit number, state what is 100 more and 100 less
Explain the strategy using place-value understanding (e.g. only the tens/hundreds digit changes)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '10 more than 342' or '100 less than 875' in their head — knowing which digit changes and which stays the same?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number to 1000, mentally, by recognising WHICH digit changes: +10 changes the tens, +100 changes the hundreds, and the other digits stay — except when a boundary forces a carry/exchange (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): mental methods and place value to 1000 (find 10/100 more or less).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.8 'mentally add 10 or 100 to, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100-900'.
• Operational details — Extend the two-digit '10 more' vertical-move idea to a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where +10 steps the tens digit and +100 steps the hundreds digit while others hold. Explicitly teach the boundary cases where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (190+10, 950+100). Demand the explanation of which digit changes and why.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): finds 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing, using a chart. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): does it mentally for any number to 1000 and names the changing digit. Tier C (age 8, extending): handles roll-over boundaries (190+10, 890+100) and explains the exchange.
bestPractices: Extend the two-digit pattern: +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, others unchanged — make the 'which digit?' question explicit.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so the child selects a new tens- or hundreds-row and physically sees one digit change.
Teach boundary roll-overs deliberately (190+10=200, 950+100=1050 later) as the interesting cases, not exceptions to memorise.
Contrast +10 vs +100 side by side so the child tracks different columns.
Insist on the reasoning ('the hundreds digit goes up by one, tens and ones stay') to keep it place-value based, not counting.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (change one row = change one digit)
H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 10 or one 100)
0-1000 number line with ±10 and ±100 hops
100-square generalisation / number grid
Base-ten flats/rods for the concrete +100 / +10 move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding 100 but stepping the tens).
Failing at boundaries — 190 + 10 giving '1100' or '190' unchanged instead of 200.
Counting on in ones instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 10 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, so mishandling the carry when a column rolls over.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number up to 1000, mentally, by reasoning about which digit changes. +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, and the other digits stay the same \u2014 except at a boundary where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200, where the tens roll 9\u21920 and carry into the hundreds). Learners should name which digit changes and explain why, keeping the method place-value based rather than counting in ones.

activities.title: Digit stepper: watch one column respond
feedback: If the wrong column is predicted: name explicitly which column '10 more' and '100 more' act on, add the matching base-ten piece (one ten or one hundred), and watch only that column move.
If a learner counts on in ones to reach the answer, prompt: 'Can you jump straight to the column that changes instead of counting?'
Reinforce correct reasoning by restating it: 'The hundreds digit goes up by one; tens and ones stay.'
activities.rationale: Making the 'which digit?' question explicit and showing exactly one column respond to one operation builds place-value reasoning rather than rote counting. An interactive chart where the affected digit highlights and ticks while others are locked can make the mechanism concrete; a number-line view showing \u00b110/\u00b1100 hops is an optional alternative representation. These interaction examples illustrate the mechanism and are not required mechanisms \u2014 base-ten counters or a paper chart reach the same insight.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils develop mental place-value methods to 1000, including finding 10 or 100 more or less.
learnerActions: Start with a three-digit number shown in an H|T|O place-value chart (e.g. 638).
Predict which digit will change before pressing +100, then press it and check: only the hundreds digit ticks up (638\u2192738) while tens and ones stay fixed.
Repeat with +10, -10, -100 on several numbers, each time saying aloud which column changes and which stay the same.
Contrast +10 and +100 side by side on the same starting number to track that they act on different columns.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding/subtracting 10 acts on the tens column and adding/subtracting 100 acts on the hundreds column; when no column rolls over (as with 638), the other digits hold still. This is a place-value jump, not counting on in ones. Boundary cases such as 190 + 10 come in the next activity.

activities.title: Boundary roll-overs: when a column fills up
feedback: If a learner writes a malformed number (190+10 = '1100' or '190' unchanged; 10 more than 695 = '6,105'): don't reteach the whole idea \u2014 rehearse the single roll on a number line or base-ten mat, e.g. 305\u2192295 (a ten taken by exchanging one hundred for ten tens), 695\u2192705 (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens make a new hundred, hundreds 6\u21927, ones stay 5).
If a learner assumes only one digit ever changes: show them the carry/borrow so they see a second column move when a column overflows.
Confirm correct regrouping: '950 + 100 fills the hundreds, so it rolls into a new thousands column: 1050.'
activities.rationale: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case and are best met deliberately rather than treated as exceptions. Seeing or physically working a cascade \u2014 the tens rolling 9\u21920 while a carry moves leftward, or exchanging base-ten pieces \u2014 makes the carry/borrow visible. Base-ten counters and a 0-1000 number line give concrete and linear views of the same jump.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs (e.g. 190+10) are the key teaching case and should be made explicit rather than treated as exceptions.
learnerActions: Start at 190 and find 10 more. Watch (or work out on a base-ten mat/number line) the tens roll 9\u21920 and a ten carry up to make one more hundred, so 190 becomes 200.
Find 10 less than 305: the tens are 0, so a hundred must be exchanged for ten tens before removing one \u2014 305, 295.
Find 10 more than 695: the tens fill up (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens), which rolls over to make a new hundred, so the hundreds go 6\u21927 and the ones stay 5 \u2014 695 becomes 705.
Find 100 more than 950 and decide whether the answer is still a three-digit number (it becomes 1050, which rolls into a new thousands column).

For each, say which digits moved and why, e.g. for 190 + 10: 'the tens filled up, so they rolled to 0 and added one to the hundreds'; for 305 - 10: 'there were no tens, so I exchanged a hundred for ten tens and took one away'; for 950 + 100: 'the hundreds filled up, so they rolled to 0 and made one thousand.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule 'only one digit changes' has a meaningful exception: when a column reaches its limit (a 9 going up, or a 0 going down), it rolls over and carries/borrows into the next column. These boundary cases are the interesting core of the skill, not exceptions to memorise.

activities.title: Fluency practice with boundary items
feedback: For plain-case errors adjusting the wrong place (100 more than 456 \u2192 466): re-name which column the operation acts on and redo with the matching base-ten piece (the answer is 556).
For boundary errors: rehearse just the single roll, not the whole concept.

Use probing questions to check reasoning, e.g. '10 less than 305 \u2014 what happens to the tens and the hundreds?', 'Which digit changes when you find 100 more? Does any other digit move?', '100 more than 950 \u2014 is the answer still a three-digit number?'
activities.rationale: Scored practice can consolidate a fluency skill after understanding is built, and deliberately mixing boundary items checks that learners handle regrouping rather than mechanically bumping one digit. Practice items assess and reinforce; they should follow, not replace, the conceptual work above.
learnerActions: Answer quick fill-in items: '100 more than 638 = __', '10 less than 305 = __', '100 more than 950 = __'.
Answer 'which digit changes?' when finding 100 more (or 10 less) for a given number.
Mix plain cases (456 + 100) with boundary cases (190 + 10, 695 + 10, 305 - 10) so the two are not predictable.
Optionally use a slider on a 0-1000 line to land on answers and self-check.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the place-value reasoning is understood, the skill can become quick mental recall, applied reliably even when a boundary forces a regroup.

constraints: Fill-in and multiple-choice practice consolidates and checks fluency but should follow conceptual work with a chart, counters, or number line; recognition-only responses do not by themselves build the place-value reasoning or the explanation of which digit changes.

A static annotated chart can serve as a reference for which digit +10/+100 changes, but learners need to carry out the transformation (physically, with counters, or interactively) to experience the roll-over; treat a fixed image as a reference scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Always require learners to explain which digit changes and why, so the method stays place-value based rather than counting on in ones.

Interactive highlights, locked digits, animated carries, number-line toggles, timed rounds, and sliders are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same insight can be reached with base-ten counters, a Gattegno/place-value chart, or a paper number line.

Tier the work: emerging learners find 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing using a chart; secure learners do it mentally for any number to 1000 and name the changing digit; extending learners handle genuine roll-over boundaries (190+10, 950+100) and explain the exchange.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Compare and order numbers to 1000 with >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones. Directly extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to a three-place, most-significant-digit-first procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.4 'compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols'.
• Operational details — Generalise 'compare the biggest place first' to three columns using aligned builds and a place-value chart; only drop to the next column when the current column ties. Stress-test with same-hundreds pairs (352 vs 358), digit-swap traps (352 vs 325) and different-length comparisons (99 vs 100). Move from pairs to ordering sets and to number-line placement.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): compares three-digit numbers with different hundreds using a build. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): orders a set to 1000 and states 'hundreds first, then tens, then ones'. Tier C (age 8, extending): resolves same-hundreds and mixed-length cases and justifies via place value, not digit count.

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones, descending a column only when the current one ties and stopping at the first place where the digits differ. Core practice uses aligned place-value builds with a left-to-right scan, trap pairs (same-hundreds, digit-swap, mixed-length, internal-zero), set ordering, and number-line placement.

activities.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
feedback: If a learner judges 358 > 372 because 8 > 2, point back to the hundreds: 3 hundreds vs 3 hundreds tie, so move to the tens where 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.
When the hundreds tie (352 vs 358), prompt: 'Hundreds are equal, so which place decides next?' then compare the tens, then the ones.
For 99 vs 100, align by place: 100 has 1 hundred while 99 has 0 hundreds, so 100 is larger. The extra digit matters because it stands for a higher place.
For 305 vs 350, highlight the internal zero: hundreds tie, then compare the tens (0 vs 5), so 305 < 350.
If the reasoning is right but the symbol is reversed, re-anchor: the open side faces the larger number; read the whole statement aloud to check.
activities.rationale: Comparison to 1000 is a left-to-right decision procedure; acting on aligned builds and scanning H→T→O makes visible where the decision is settled and generalises the known two-digit rule by adding one column.

Place a >, =, or < card between them, with the open side facing the larger number.
Work left to right: decide at the hundreds first; only if the hundreds tie, move to the tens; only if the tens tie, move to the ones. Stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Say aloud which place settled the decision and why.
Repeat with trap pairs: same-hundreds (352 vs 358), digit-swap (352 vs 325), and mixed-length (99 vs 100).
Then order a set of 4-5 numbers smallest to largest and place numbers on a 0-1000 number line.
activities.intendedInsight: When the numbers are lined up by place, the comparison is always decided at the first (highest) place where the two numbers differ; move down to the next place only on a tie. A bigger ones digit does not by itself make a number larger. A whole number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is larger because it reaches a higher place, as when 100 has a hundred and 99 does not.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Place Value to 1000
topic.description: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
evidence: Solve a problem that requires identifying how many hundreds, tens, or ones are in a number
Apply place-value knowledge to a practical context (e.g. counting money in pounds)
Explain the strategy used to solve a place-value problem
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told 'I have 4 hundreds, 3 tens, and 7 ones — what number is that?', can they put it together and tell you 437?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8 (META). Solve number and practical problems using place value to 1000 — e.g. 'how many tens in 340?', money in pounds and pence, or 'my number has 4 hundreds and 7 ones and no tens, what is it?'. Applying three-digit place value flexibly, not learning it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'solve number problems and practical problems involving these ideas' (three-digit place value).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT / 2.MD.8 apply place value and use it in money and measurement contexts; problem-solving with base-ten reasoning.
• Operational details — Pose varied problems that reward partitioning, 'how many tens/hundreds', missing-digit clues and real contexts (money, measures). Model with part-whole/bar models and place-value counters; think aloud then hand reasoning to the child. Emphasise flexible partitioning (340 = 34 tens = 3 hundreds 4 tens) and inverse/missing-value reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): solves a one-step place-value problem with a model. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): answers 'how many tens in 340' and missing-digit clues, explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 8, extending): tackles multi-step/real-context problems and reasons flexibly about non-canonical partitions.
bestPractices: Pose genuine problems (how-many-tens, missing-digit clues, money/measures) that reward place-value reasoning, not routine recall.
Model with part-whole / bar models and place-value counters, thinking aloud, then transfer the explaining to the child.
Stress flexible partitioning: 340 is 3 hundreds 4 tens AND 34 tens AND 300 + 40 — choose the useful view.
Use money as a natural place-value context (£/10p/1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones).
Include missing-value / inverse problems to build reasoning beyond direct calculation.

Place-value counters and H|T|O chart
Money (pounds/tens of pence/pence) as a place-value context
0-1000 number line for jump/benchmark reasoning
Arrow cards for flexible partitioning
commonMisconceptions: Only seeing canonical partition (340 = 300 + 40) and missing '34 tens'.
Counting in ones instead of using place-value structure.
Mishandling internal zeros in problem numbers (407).

Not mapping money/measure contexts onto place-value columns.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, solve number and practical problems using three-digit place value to 1000, applying it flexibly rather than first learning it. The central objective is flexible re-unitising: seeing that the SAME number can be decomposed many equivalent ways (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens = 34 tens = 300 + 40) and choosing the view that fits the problem. Children work 'how many tens/hundreds' questions, missing-digit clues (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones give 407), and money/measure contexts, explaining and checking their reasoning.

activities.title: Place-value problem workbench: re-unitise to answer
feedback: If the child gives only the canonical partition (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens), prompt: 'Can you exchange each hundred for ten tens? How many tens altogether now?'
When the child exchanges correctly, confirm that 34 tens and 3 hundreds 4 tens are the same number seen two ways.
If the child counts in ones, redirect to the place-value structure: 'Use the hundreds and tens rather than counting each one.'
For 'how many hundreds in 680?', accept 6 hundreds (with 8 tens left over) and discuss why this count is not a whole re-unitising like 340 to 34 tens.
activities.rationale: A manipulable problem bench lets the child physically partition, regroup and read off answers, making the re-unitising move visible rather than guessed. Live recomputation (hundred-flats visibly breaking into ten tens-rods) is intended to make the equivalence concrete. This is one suitable, proposed approach for a problem-solving (META) topic; physical base-ten pieces or arrow cards serve the same purpose without a screen.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Read a problem card such as 'How many tens are in 340?'
Build 340 with place-value pieces (three hundred-flats, four tens-rods) or arrow cards.
Exchange each hundred-flat for ten tens-rods on an exchange pad and watch 340 reassemble as 34 tens-rods, then read off the answer: 34 tens.
Repeat for another number (e.g. how many tens in 350? how many hundreds in 680?) and say which decomposition you used.
Name the strategy you used each time ('I re-unitised the hundreds into tens').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be re-unitised into equivalent decompositions; you pick the view that answers the question, and you can check by rebuilding the original number.

activities.title: Money and measures as place-value columns
feedback: If the child doesn't connect pounds to hundreds, lay the money beside place-value counters so the one-to-one mapping is visible.
For £4.07, check the internal zero: 'There are no 10p coins here — how do we show that in the tens column?'
Confirm answers by rebuilding: '407 pence — can you make that back into pounds and pence?'
activities.rationale: Money is a natural, real context where place-value columns transfer directly, and it surfaces the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p). Real contexts reward place-value reasoning over routine recall.
sourceClaims: Place-value reasoning is applied in problem contexts including money and measurement (2.NBT / 2.MD.8).
learnerActions: Solve a money problem such as '£4.07 = how many pence?' using a money tray (pounds, 10p, 1p).
Counting the amount in pence, map pounds onto hundreds (£1 = 100p), 10p onto tens, and 1p onto ones, lining them up in place-value columns.
Work a small shopping total using the same columns you used for whole numbers.
State how the money columns mirror hundreds/tens/ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Money (pounds / 10p / 1p) mirrors the hundreds/tens/ones structure, so a shopping total is solved with the identical place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Missing-digit and missing-value clues
feedback: If the child writes 47 for 'four hundreds, no tens, seven ones', ask: 'Where do the hundreds go? What holds the tens place when there are none?'
For inverse problems, prompt 'what is the number made of?' before any calculation.
Confirm by reading the built number aloud and checking it matches every part of the clue (34 tens and no ones gives 340; 34 tens make 340).
activities.rationale: Missing-digit and inverse problems build reasoning beyond direct calculation and are intended to address inverse-blindness and mishandling of internal zeros, both common difficulties.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
learnerActions: Read a clue such as 'I have 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones — what number am I?' and build the number (407).
Honour the placeholder: put no tens pieces in the tens column but keep the column, and write a 0 digit there when recording, so the number is written correctly as 407, not 47.
Work an inverse/missing-value problem, e.g. '__ tens make 340' or 'a number has 34 tens and no ones — what is it?'
Explain how you knew where each digit belonged.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is a two-way tool: you can reason backwards from a description to the number, and internal zeros act as placeholders that must be honoured.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: how did you decide?
feedback: If the child insists '350 IS 3 hundreds and 5 tens, that's it', model several equivalent builds of 350 with base-ten pieces (exchange a hundred for ten tens) and name each as the same number seen differently.
If the child reaches for a taught calculation first, don't supply a procedure — ask 'what is 350 made of?' so composition drives the method.
Treat this as eliciting reasoning, not scoring: surface the thinking rather than grading it.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning suits a META topic for eliciting strategy. At 7-8, pairing talk with an external model (pieces, arrow cards) is usually more productive than sustained talk alone, so keep manipulatives available during the discussion. A dialogue can elicit and probe reasoning but does not by itself build the hands-on re-unitising move.
sourceClaims: Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a riddle or problem and explain, step by step, how you worked it out.

Answer probes such as: 'How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?', 'Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?', 'What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?'
Test whether the same thinking helps for 'how many tens are in 352' and say what changes.
Justify your chosen decomposition and check it by rebuilding the number.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a chosen decomposition fits — and to check it — shows place value is held as a flexible strategy, not a single fixed label.

activities.title: Consolidation problems and worked reference
feedback: For a fill-in or multiple-choice item, if wrong, send the child back to build the number and re-unitise rather than restating the answer.
Use the worked example to prompt the next reasoning step, not to supply the result.
Encourage the child to explain the strategy after answering, as the evidence asks for ('explain the strategy used').
activities.rationale: Structured items and a worked-example anchor support consolidation and self-correction. Recognition and recall items assess and reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on construction.
learnerActions: Answer a mix of items: 'how many tens in 340?', '£4.07 = __ pence', 'which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones?', and match each problem to its useful partition.
Attempt a multi-step word problem in a real context (e.g. money).
Use a worked example of a how-many-tens problem as a reference: step through the reasoning when stuck, rather than copying the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Varied practice consolidates flexible partitioning and lets the child recognise which decomposition a given problem rewards.

constraints: Target the actual objective — flexible re-unitising and problem solving — not routine recall of 'hundreds, tens, ones'.

Recognition-only items (multiple choice, matching) assess and consolidate but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation that are the goal; pair them with construction and spoken reasoning.
A worked example is a reference, not varied problem practice; it cannot replace the child working new problems.
Keep money/measure mappings honest: pounds / 10p / 1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones, and the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p) must be handled explicitly.
Honour placeholders: a clue like '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' must build 407, not 47.

Physical base-ten pieces, arrow cards and screen models all make re-unitising visible; none is uniquely necessary. On-screen live recolouring/exchange is an optional way to show the move, not a requirement.
The evidence expects the child to explain the strategy, so build explanation into every activity.

Where a 'how many hundreds/tens' question does not re-unitise to a whole count (e.g. 680 as hundreds gives 6 hundreds and 8 tens over), treat the remainder honestly rather than forcing a clean single number.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Reading and writing numbers to 1000
topic.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
evidence: Read a three-digit numeral aloud correctly
Write a three-digit number in words (e.g. 'three hundred and forty-two')
Write a number in expanded form (e.g. 600 + 30 + 7)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 1,000 — both as numerals and in words — like reading '642' as 'six hundred and forty-two'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Read and write numbers to 1000 in three registers — numerals (342), number names ('three hundred and forty-two') and expanded form (300 + 40 + 2) — and move fluently between them. This is the LANGUAGE/notation face of three-digit place value.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.3 'read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form'.
• Operational details — Teach the three registers as mutually-translatable views anchored to a build. Attend hard to the spoken-to-written mapping ('and', the hundreds word, internal zeros): 'three hundred and six' → 306, not 3006 or 36. Practise both directions (read a numeral aloud; write a spoken number). Expanded form is the bridge that exposes each digit's value.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): reads/writes three-digit numerals with no internal zero. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): translates among numeral, words and expanded form including one internal zero. Tier C (age 8, extending): writes tricky spoken numbers (306, 340) correctly and explains the expanded form's link to place value.
bestPractices: Treat numeral / words / expanded form as three views of one number and translate in all directions, always tied to a build.
Target the spoken→written danger zone: the hundreds word, the connective 'and', and internal zeros (306, 640).
Use expanded form (300+40+2) as the explicit bridge from words to place value.
Dictate numbers for children to write (and vice versa) so both encode and decode directions are fluent.
Sequence from no-zero → one internal zero → trailing zero to isolate the hard cases.
keyRepresentations: The three registers side by side: numeral | words | expanded form
Place-value chart / arrow cards linking words to columns
Base-ten build under each register as the anchor
Number-word cards (hundred, and, -ty, teen) for constructing names
0-1000 number line for locating the number named
commonMisconceptions: Writing what you hear literally: 'three hundred and six' → 3006 or 30006.
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (340 written as 34; 306 as 36).
Mis-ordering words vs digits, or omitting the hundreds word.
Confusing teen and -ty words within the tens part (forty vs fourteen).
Treating expanded form as separate numbers (300, 40, 2) rather than a partition of one number.

learn.summary: Ages 7-8: read and write numbers to 1000 across three registers — numerals (342), number names ('three hundred and forty-two') and expanded form (300 + 40 + 2) — and translate fluently in both directions. The hardest cases are the spoken→written mapping and internal/placeholder zeros (306, 340, 305). Expanded form acts as an explicit bridge from number names to place value. Core activities give learners genuine two-way production (encode and decode) anchored to a base-ten build; a static reference wall and light oral reading are preserved as scaffolds with stated limits.

activities.title: Three-pane number translator (build, type, name)
feedback: If the words-to-numeral entry comes out too long (e.g. 30042 for 'three hundred and forty-two'), build 342 with base-ten blocks and place each part into a hundreds/tens/ones frame so parts land in columns rather than being appended.
For a placeholder-zero number, show 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones: the 0 holds the tens place so the 3 stays in hundreds; contrast 35, 305 and 350 directly.
Optionally, a 'dictation' mode can speak a trap number (306, 340) for the child to write, flagging a wrong or missing internal zero against the empty column in the build.
activities.rationale: Translating among the three registers is production in both directions, which a two-way build+type+name tool exercises directly while the base-ten model anchors meaning. Expanded form is used as the bridge from number names to place value, and the live base-ten column makes the placeholder-zero rule visible.
sourceClaims: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form (2.NBT.3).
Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
Year 3 pupils should 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
learnerActions: Work with three linked views of one number side by side: a numeral display, a word-tile builder, and an expanded-form strip, with a base-ten build (flats/rods/cubes) shown beneath.

Change any one view and watch the others and the blocks rebuild: assemble the word-tiles 'three hundred and forty-two' and confirm 342 appears alongside 300 + 40 + 2 and three flats, four rods, two cubes.
Translate deliberately in BOTH directions: read a shown numeral and build its words; and start from spoken/word form and write the numeral.
Sequence difficulty: start with no-zero numbers (342), then one internal zero (306), then a trailing zero (340).
activities.intendedInsight: Numeral, words and expanded form are three views of ONE number; expanded form reveals each digit's place value, and the empty column shows why a placeholder zero must be written (306, not 36 or 3006).

activities.title: Two-way translation practice (write it, name it, expand it)
feedback: If expanded form of 637 is written as 600 + 3 + 7, read each digit with its place ('3 tens = 30') and check the parts add back to 637.
If 305 is read or written as 'thirty-five'/35 or 3005, re-show 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones and contrast 35, 305, 350.
Check teen vs -ty words in the tens part (forty vs fourteen) when a name is miswritten.
activities.rationale: Reading and writing to 1000 is a two-way production and checking skill; targeted practice in both directions, including the internal-zero danger zone, builds and verifies fluency. This format both teaches by practice and can check the same skills.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form (2.NBT.3).
Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
learnerActions: Write a spoken or word-form number as a numeral (e.g. write 'six hundred and forty' as 640).
Write a given numeral in words (e.g. write 306 as 'three hundred and six').
Complete expanded form from a numeral (e.g. 485 = 400 + __ + 5) and the reverse.
Match numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form for a set of numbers, deliberately including internal-zero and trailing-zero cases (305, 340).
Decide the correct written form among plausible errors for internal-zero numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Both encode (spoken/words → numeral) and decode (numeral → words) directions become reliable, especially for the zero traps and the tens digit's place value.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number in three registers
feedback: Point back to the anchor when a learner omits the hundreds word or mis-orders words and digits: match each spoken chunk to its column.
Use the 306 flap to re-explain the placeholder whenever an internal zero is dropped.
activities.rationale: A fixed, aligned reference consolidates the correspondence between registers and names the placeholder-zero rule. As a reference scaffold it does not by itself elicit the two-way writing/reading production, so it is paired with the translation activities.
sourceClaims: Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
learnerActions: Study a fixed anchor card showing 342 as numeral, words and expanded form at once, with a base-ten build.
Tap the words to highlight the matching digits and expanded parts (where an interactive display is available).
Open a 306 'card flap' that explains why the 0 is written in the tens place.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing all three registers of the same number aligned, with the placeholder zero explained, gives a stable mental model to refer back to.

activities.title: Read-it-back oral warm-up
feedback: If 'three hundred and six' is misheard as a longer number, slow the chunks (three hundred / and / six) and match each to a column.

• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that the multiples of 100 (100, 200 … 900) are 'some hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones' — 300 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. This isolates the hundreds column and reinforces two placeholder zeros.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'; three-digit place value (hundreds, tens, ones).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1b 'the numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three… nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones)'.
• Operational details — Build multiples of 100 from hundred-flats only, pairing with skip-counting in 100s and placement on a 0-1000 number line. Emphasise the DOUBLE placeholder (two zeros) and connect to the analogous decade structure (300 is to hundreds what 30 is to tens). Read and write them and locate them as landmark numbers.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 500 with 5 flats, says 'five hundreds'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): reads/writes any multiple of 100 and explains the two zeros. Tier C (age 8, extending): places multiples of 100 on a 0-1000 line and links them to the tens/decade pattern.

Explicitly parallel the decade pattern: 300 is 'three hundreds' as 30 is 'three tens' — the ×10 self-similarity again.
Use the 0-1000 number line to treat multiples of 100 as landmark/benchmark numbers for later estimation and rounding.
Contrast 300 with 30 and 3, and with 303/330, to sharpen the meaning of each zero.

• Operational details — Extend the two-digit column model to three columns (H|T|O) with base-ten flats/rods/cubes, place-value counters and arrow cards, keeping build + name + expanded form (300+60+2) synchronised. Give heavy attention to internal zeros (706, 350) because that is where three-digit place value breaks down. Partition and recombine flexibly.

Tier B (age 7-8, secure): partitions any three-digit number into 300+60+2 and handles an internal zero (706). learnerActions: Answer value-of-digit items: 'What is the 3 in 362 worth?' (300).
Match a built representation to its numeral, including 706 and 350 zero traps.
For each answer, give a reason: why is 706 different from 76 — what is the 0 doing?
Diagnostic: write 706 and explain what each digit is worth, what the 0 is doing, and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Once a number is built, learners can be checked on whether they read digits by place, handle the placeholder zero, and partition flexibly; the reason tier reveals whether the structure is understood or digits are read at face value.

constraints: Keep concrete build, number name and expanded form in lockstep for every number so the three views stay connected.
Give heavy, explicit attention to internal and trailing zeros (706, 350, 300) — this is where three-digit place value commonly breaks down.
Recognition and matching items check structure but do not elicit independent construction; include build and partition tasks where the learner produces the number and states digit values.
The static labelled anchor is a reference scaffold: it cannot let a learner build arbitrary numbers or watch the placeholder emerge, so pair it with active building.
Dialogue is a supplement for eliciting a learner's reasoning; it does not itself produce the physical build, so place it to follow hands-on building.

Flat paper/card items such as overlay cards have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal notation; a screen bench with a live readout is one option, not a requirement, and physical materials can carry the activity equally.
Extend the two-digit model deliberately so the hundreds place is seen as the same idea, not a brand-new rule.

Additional source representations — place-value counters (100/10/1) in labelled columns, a 0–1000 number line, a part-whole model, and a Gattegno chart — may support the same place-value structure and can substitute for or supplement the flats/rods/cubes and arrow cards; the alternative non-canonical partition 362 = 340 + 22 is another valid flexibility example.

The original row labelled 3D interactive as poor fit, asserting a third dimension 'adds load, not insight'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it is omitted as a universal law and treated only as a design preference for a planar place-value layout.

The original recommendation framed the build as 'defeating' the 7006/76 error. Softened: building and explaining the placeholder can address this error, but the sources do not establish that any single artefact defeats a misconception.
